Chapter 7: Navigating Mistakes, Repair, and Recommitment
You know, no journey of growth is ever completely free from mistakes. In antiracist practice, slip-ups are bound to happen—sometimes we say the wrong thing, sometimes our actions don't quite measure up, and, even with the best intentions, we might end up causing harm. So, what do you do when things go off track? Well, this chapter is all about how to respond in those moments, and why repair and recommitment matter so much.
Here’s something to keep in mind: mistakes aren’t the end of the story. In fact, they’re actually chances to learn and connect more deeply. It’s not about never making an error—it’s about how you handle it when you do.
Think about learning a new language. At first, you’re going to stumble, maybe even say something embarrassing. But every mistake? That’s an opportunity to get better. The same goes for antiracism. Missteps aren’t a reason to quit—they’re just part of the process.
So, when harm happens, there are a few steps that can really help with making things right:
First, acknowledge the impact. It’s all about focusing on how your actions affected others, rather than jumping in to defend your intentions.
Next, offer a sincere apology. Leave out the excuses and justifications—just let it be real.
Then, listen and learn. Be open to feedback. Try to really understand what went wrong, even if it’s uncomfortable.
After that, make amends. Take some concrete steps to address the harm and make sure it doesn’t happen again.
And finally, recommit to the work. Let the experience fuel your motivation to keep learning and taking action.
Imagine this: someone lets you know that a comment you made was offensive. Your first reaction might be to explain yourself, or maybe even brush it off. But what if, instead, you paused, listened, apologized, and asked how you could do better? That small shift can turn a tough moment into an opening for trust and growth.
There’s another piece to all of this—self-compassion. It’s easy to get stuck in shame or guilt when you mess up, but those feelings don’t really help. The goal here is to stay engaged, keep learning, and remember that antiracism isn’t about being perfect. It’s a lifelong journey, not a pass-or-fail test.
So, the next time you stumble, remember: it’s not about avoiding mistakes—it’s about how you show up to repair, and how you choose to move forward.
